abstract: Mobility hubs involve co-locating shared bikes/e-bikes, cars, e-scooters or similar  modes. They are often close to transit and other facilities, such as charging stations or parcel lockers, with the aim being to provide alternatives to (petrol-driven) car ownership and support more sustainable travel behaviours.  A range of signage, information displays and branding appproaches for mobility hubs have already been developed by practitioners, but best practices are unclear.  As well, tools to help create mobility hubs out of existing (and already co-located) services appear to be lacking. This paper reports a synthesis of existing practices, and development of software tools for creating maps and informational displays for mobility hubs in any location. Are there multiple mobility offerings in close proximity in your community? These tools, a printer and somewhere hang a poster might be all that is needed to spread the word.

# Introduction
Shared mobility hubs 
are places where a range of modes 
and sometimes other facilities 
are provided to support more sustainable travel. 
They often include shared electric cars, 
bikes, cargobikes, e-bikes, e-scooters or 
other micro-mobility services. 
Together, these might help 
support shifts towards more walking and cycling, 
transit use, 
and otherwise improve the sustainability of transport systems 
through providing options for those 
(more occasional) trips that are difficult without a private car.  

Many mobility hubs have already been implemented, 
but with signage, maps and other informational material 
created by individual agencies on a site-by-site basis. 
Current and best practices are unclear. 
As well, the graphic design, 
mapping and similar effort 
needed to develop such signs 
for each site 
may limit the ability 
for practitioners 
to keep information up to date, 
trial new hubs, 
or use bottom-up implementation approaches to 
create hubs where shared or other modes 
are already in close proximity. 

This paper aims to explore and better understand 
mobility hub information provision, 
and to develop tools to support practitioners. 
It reports findings from case research 
examining existing practices 
at a selection of mobility hubs. 
Also reported are findings from design-based research 
that develops software tools for producing 
maps and information displays 
for mobility hubs, 
based on both replication and synthesis 
of industry practices. 
The rest of
this paper is structured as follows: the next section outlines the context for this study. The research methodology is then described, followed by presentation of the results. 
These are then briefly discussed 
prior to a conclusion that 
includes identification of directions for future research.

# Research context
An early version of the mobility hub concept 
was developed in Toronto's "Big Move" transport plan [@Metrolinx:2008aa] 
in the late 2000s, 
which used to the term  
to denote selected major regional transit stations 
around which landuses would be intensified 
and where intermodal transfers 
would be facilitated [@Salsberg:2010aa, @Engel-Yan:2012aa]. 
In the intervening years there has been rapid developments 
in shared micro-mobility and 
vehicle electrification, 
such that shared bike, 
e-bike and e-scooter 
systems are common. 
Various problems have emerged, however, 
including inappropriate parking of dockless vehicles blocking footpath; 
the environmental and other impacts associated 
with rebalancing and battery swapping; 
the risk of fires at recharging facilities; 
and safety challenges associated with user behaviour 
(see for example, @Meigs:2023aa, @Zhang:2022aa and @Bozzi:2021aa).
Consolidating shared and micro-mobility services 
into mobility hubs may help to resolve some of these challenges.  
Shared *electric* mobility hubs where 
each shared e-car, e-bike or other vehicle has 
its own powered parking space 
might eliminate the need for rebalancing or battery swapping entirely. 
This is case at sites in Galway and other parts of Ireland that are part 
of the current ongoing 
Electric shaRed mOBility hUbS Trial (ROBUST) [@ROBUST:2025aa], 
of which the research described in this paper is a part.

 
Mobility hubs, 
however, 
appear likely to continue to come in many forms, 
and incorporate a wide range of 
vehicles, facilities and other services. 
Some guidance is provided by a definition recently developed 
from a review of the literature,
that highlights the need for 
"integration", 
"seamless, flexible connection" and
"...an enjoyable experience for travelers" [@Roukouni:2023aa].
<!-- ^[*“A shared mobility hub is a place where different transport modes are integrated seamlessly, promoting efficient and sustainable urban mobility. Emphasis is given on shared mobility options such as bikes, scooters and cars. Connection with public transport (transit) is desirable but not necessary. The integration between mobility suppliers is important to provide a seamless, flexible connection at these transfer points. Ensuring an enjoyable experience for travelers is a crucial part of the hub concept as well, and therefore the hub should be considered not just as a transfer node but as a place where a variety of services come together, such as logistics services or restaurants”* (Roukouni et al. 2023).]-->
How such integration, user experience and seamlessness 
might be achieved, implemented and maintained by practitioners 
appears unclear.  

Signs, maps and information displays 
would seem to be 
and important consideration 
when creating a new mobility hub (whatever its form).
More broadly, 
‘Movement and Place’ and ‘Complete Streets’ [@Delbosc:2018aa], 
and tactical urbanism approaches [@Lydon:2012aa; @Lydon:2015aa; @Davidson:2013aa; @Blumgart:2016ab; @Morhayim:2012aa; Longhurst:2015aa] 
suggest way to challenge prevailing naratives about road space allocation, 
give communities greater power over (their own) urban environments, 
and demonstrate the potential of change. 
Bottom-up and incremental approaches, 
‘pop-ups’ 
and more formal trials 
have also been found to be 
pragmatic strategies 
for building legitimacy *through* implementation [@Reynolds:2021ab].  
In the context of mobility hubs, 
however,
these might rely on 
rapid prototyping, 
iterative co-design or 
other approaches 
for which practitioners, 
tactical urbanists 
and others 
might to need adopt a   
'do it yourself' 
attitude when it comes 
to developing information displays 
and supporting maps. 
As of yet, there does not appear to be 
standarised approaches 
for providing such information, 
or a clear understanding of best practices. 
Nor are there tools that might allow  
such best practices to be 
quickly and easily adapted to local contexts, 
and for updates to be made as a mobility hub 
or its surrounding urban environment changes over time. 
The next section, therefore 
describes the case- and design-based 
research methodology 
adopted in this study 
to (at least start) 
filling this gap in knowledge.  


# Methodology

The research described in this paper 
is part of the larger ROBUST project 
on shared electric mobility hubs, 
which was briefly discussed above.  
This component of the project 
aims to improve understanding of 
'best practices' in 
in mobility hub signage and information provision, 
and to develop tools to support mobility hub implementation. 
Research questions relate to: 
*how* information is provided at and about mobility hubs? 
*how* information at and about mobility hubs might ideally be provided? 
(i.e. best practices) and 
*how* can such best practices be made generally applicable?*^[More formally, 
the (null) hypothesis tested in this study is that it is *not* possible to develop software tools for generating mobility hub information displays that reflect best practices and are generally applicable to other sites.] 

## Study design
The study designed 
adopts 
the Double Diamond design process [@UK-Design-Council:0aa]. 
@Coxon:2018aa and @Coxon:2021ab identify 
this as a suitable tool 
for design-based research seeking to 
develop solutions to mobility problems. 
The Double Diamond process involves 
iteration across four phases: 
1. *Discovery*, 2. *Definition*, 3. *Development* and 4. *Delivery*. 
These phases alternate 
between divergent (1 \& 3) and convergent (2 \& 4) approaches, 
although the overall process 
is iterative 
and may involve 
multiple passes through each phase. 

Here the *Discovery* and *Development* 
phases utilised a case research approach, 
which @Denscombe:2007aa, @Yin:2018ab and others 
identify as being especially effective
for when: theory development 
is at an early stage; 
research questions relate to 'how' or 'why'; and
when exploring phenomena within real-world contexts. 


## Participants, Material and Instruments
The authors were the only participants 
in the research reported in this paper. 
As discussed in the conclusion to this paper 
further research as part of the ROBUST project 
is expected to involve 
mobility hub users, stakeholders and others 
in testing, co-design and continued iteration. 
These, however, are beyond the scope of this paper.  

Material for the study was drawn from: 
photos taken during sites visits 
made by the lead author in the *Discovery* phase; 
and mapping, imagery and other online resources. 
Open Street Map datasets provided an input 
for the *Development* phase.  
 
Instruments included synthesis tables 
for cross-case comparisons. 
These were developed as per @Miles:1994aa. 
*Development* used the R programming language to 
replicate the informational display styles discovered 
at the leading cases (Bristol and Birmingham). 
Package development during the *Delivery* phase 
was guided by @wickham2023r. 

## Procedure and analysis
In the *Discovery* phase 
cases were selected from the larger sample available at https://www.como.org.uk/mobility-hubs/built-andplanned-hubs. 
Inclusion was somewhat constrained by logistics, 
but guided by the case research methodological literature (see @Eisenhardt:1989aa, @Stuart:2002aa, @Voss:2002aa, @Eisenhardt:2007aa, @Denscombe:2007aa, @Barratt:2011aa, @Yin:2018ab and others). 
Selected cases included the leading examples of
the mobility hubs developed by the 
West of England Mayoral Combined Authority (WEMCA, Bristol) 
and Transport for West Midlands (Birmingham). 
More representative examples from Camden Council (London) 
and the London Borough of Redbridge (Woodford and Wanstead) 
were also included to provide polar opposites for cross-case comparison. 
Within each case a small number of mobility hubs were visited 
to allow for within-case comparison^[*Redbridge*: South Woodford and High Street, Wanstead; and in *Camden*: Goldington Crescent, and Doric Way; *Bristol*: Abbey Wood, UWE Frenchay, and Gainsborough Square. *Birmingham*: Huntingtree Park and Andrew Road]. 

The *Definition* phase involved synthesis of findings 
from the site visits and about each included case. 
As per @UK-Design-Council:0aa], @Coxon:2018aa and @Coxon:2021ab, 
this provided the basis for defining the problem 
that needs to be addressed by the research outputs. 

The *Development* phase involved 
iterative software coding to 
first replicate the Bristol and Birmingham 
style of information displays. 
This replication was first undertaken for cases included in the *Discovery*, 
and then repeated to test the software 
on the contexts of 
the ROBUST hubs in Galway, Letterkenny and Dundrum. 
Finally, a combined display style 
was developed 
based on the synthesis of industry practices 
undertaken during the *Discovery* phase 
and responding to the problem developed in the *Definition* phase. 
As per @UK-Design-Council:0aa], @Coxon:2018aa and @Coxon:2021ab, 
the research also included iteration 
through all four phases^[ 
These iterations were tracked using the Git version control system, and code used in the production of this paper is available at 
[https://github.com/James-Reynolds/WP5_mobilityHubTools_papers/blob/main/ReynoldsEtAl2026_CERC.Rmd](https://github.com/James-Reynolds/WP5_mobilityHubTools_papers/blob/main/ReynoldsEtAl2026_CERC.Rmd). The software package itself is available at 
[https://github.com/James-Reynolds/mobilityHubTools](https://github.com/James-Reynolds/mobilityHubTools), and is expected to be developed further during later parts of the ROBUST project]. 
However, in the interests of clarity 
the next section presents 
the results in a linear format, 
stepping through each phase in turn.

## Discovery

from the case research^[Table notes: 1. Case study questions (column 1) are of the form 'How are details related to <COLUMN 1> at the hub communicated?' 2. 'S' denotes secure bicycle parking, such as a locker. 3. Totem denotes a free standing information pedestal. 4. Information displays ranged from small placard signs 
(South Woodford and Wanstead) 
to comprehensive totem displays and posters (Bristol and Birmingham). 
Mobility hubs in Camden lacked any information signs. 
Sites were labelled as "Mobility Hub" or "Village Hub" (South Woodford and Wanstead) and "Local Travel Point" in Birmingham. 

Where present, totems all included two maps: 
one at a local scale (within 5 minutes walk) 
and a second showing a larger area (within 15 minutes). 
These generally showed 
nearby transit, cafes, shops and 
other points of interest.  
Text descriptions of local walking and cycling routes, 
hub facilities and transit services 
were also included in the information displays in Bristol and Birmingham.  

Many of the sites had linemarking that highlighted some hub components. 
The Bristol hubs also included cube shaped indicators 
mounted on poles  
to help with finding hub components.  (see Figure \ref{fig:bristol_images_panels}, bottom right). 
 
Bicycle parking hoops were the most commonly provided feature. 
Some hubs in Camden, Bristol and Birmingham also included bicycle lockers 
or similar higher security parking. 
Seating and nearby toilets were available as part of some hubs, 
but no hubs included comprehensive shelter or access to water. 
The Bristol hubs included USB connections for phone recharging, 
and wifi internet connectivity at some locations.  

Overall, findings during the *Discovery* phase suggest that current practices 
relating to information displays at mobility hubs are inconsistent. 
Best practices appear to be represented by the totem displays 
in Bristol and Birmingham. These are generally similiar to other such displays, 
notably the Transport For London Cycles display that is close to, 
but not part of, 
the mobility hub in Doric Way, Camden (Figure \ref{fig:selected_images}, top left).  

## Definition

Findings from the case research, 
iteration through the Double Diamond phases 
and synthesis resulted 
led to the expression of the 
design problem to be addressed in this research 
in the form of: 
*five questions a mobility hub information display needs answer*. 
These are shown in Table \ref{tab:definition_details}.  
Also shown is an assessment of how each of the cases 
does (or does not) respond to each. 

```{r definition_details, eval = TRUE, echo = FALSE,  warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}

tibble(Question = c("1. What is this?", 
                    "2. Where am I?", 
                    "3. What is here?", 
                    "4. What is nearby?", 
                    "5. How can I travel from here?"),
       Purpose = c("Define current location as a mobility hub", 
                   "Identify current location", 
                   "Identify hub elements", 
                   "Identify nearby services/facilities", 
                   "Identify spatial network context"), 
       Redbridge = c("Mobility or village hub, or 'Public Space'", 
                     "Place name", 
                     "Limited", 
                     "Limited", 
                     "Not answered"), 
       Camden = c("Not answered", 
                  "Not answered", 
                  "Not answered", 
                  "Not answered", 
                  "Not answered"), 
       WEMCA = c("Not explictly answered", 
                 "Place name", 
                 "Icons, cube markers, description", 
                 "Local and regional maps, description, direction arrows", 
                 "Description of bus/bike, bike routes on area map"), 
       TWM = c("Local Travel Point", 
               "Place name", 
               "Icons, description", 
               "Local and regional maps, description, direction arrows", 
               "Description of bus routes only")) %>% 
  kable(align = "lllll",
    caption = "Defining the design problem through five questions. Authors' concept.", 
    col.names = c("Question", "Purpose", "Redbridge London", "Camden London", "WEMCA Bristol", "TWM Birmingham"))  %>% 
  kable_styling(font_size = 7) %>% 
  column_spec(1, width = "2.25cm", border_right = TRUE) %>%
  column_spec(2, width = "2.8cm", border_right = TRUE) %>%
  column_spec(3, width = "2.8cm", border_right = TRUE) %>%
  column_spec(4, width = "1.75cm", border_right = TRUE) %>%
  column_spec(5, width = "2.75cm", border_right = TRUE) %>%
  column_spec(6, width = "2.75cm", border_right = TRUE) %>%
  add_header_above(c("Problem" = 2, 
                     "Answers from cases" = 4)) 

```

The first question shown in Table \ref{tab:definition_details} 
relates to identifying a mobility hub 
as something in and of itself. 
Various terms were used in practice 
(Village Hub, Public Space, Local Travel Point), 
except in Camden (no information display) 
and Bristol (place name only). 

The second question (*Where am I?*) was answered in the cases 
either by place names (Redbridge, Bristol and Birmingham) or not at all (Camden).  For the third question (*What is here?*) the best industry practices appear to be identify hub elements through text descriptions, icons, linemarking and cube markers. Notably, hub elements were not always shown on the maps answering the fourth question (*what else is nearby?*). Answers to the final question shown in Table \ref{tab:definition_details}(*How can you travel from here?*) were similarly limited, although some information displays included text descriptions and limited mapping. 

Overall, therefore 
the *Defined* problem to be addressed by this research 
related to produce information displays 
that answer these five questions. 
Hence, the final two Double Diamond phases 
involved developing and delivering software tools 
that could create such displays 
in a totem or poster-sized format. 
Such tools also needed to include functionality 
to assist users in obtaining data and producing maps, 
but also allow user input of component elements, 
descriptive text and other details about a mobility hub.  
Finally, the software needed to be generalisable, such that it might be used to develop mobility hub informational displays elsewhere 
(i.e. beyond the cases examined in this study). 


## Development



```{r download_osm_data_function, eval=FALSE, include=TRUE, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE }

download_osm_data_by_category_function <- function(
    hub_location = hub_location, crs_local_metres = crs_local_metres, 
    key = key)
{
### Create hub locations
hub_location <- lapply(hub_location, function(x) x %>% 
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), 
           crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(crs = crs_local_metres) %>% 
  st_cast("POINT"))

place_sf <- lapply(hub_location, function(x) x %>% 
                    st_buffer(dist = 2000) %>%
                    st_transform(crs = 4326) 
                  )

placebb <- lapply(hub_location, function(x) x %>% 
                    st_buffer(dist = 2000) %>%
                    st_transform(crs = 4326) %>%
                    st_bbox()
                  )
### based on https://github.com/ropensci/osmdata/blob/main/vignettes/query-split.Rmd

split_bbox <- function (bbox, grid = 2, eps = 0.05) {
    xmin <- bbox ["x", "min"]
    ymin <- bbox ["y", "min"]
    dx <- (bbox ["x", "max"] - bbox ["x", "min"]) / grid
    dy <- (bbox ["y", "max"] - bbox ["y", "min"]) / grid

    bboxl <- list ()

    for (i in 1:grid) {
        for (j in 1:grid) {
            b <- matrix (c (
                xmin + ((i - 1 - eps) * dx),
                ymin + ((j - 1 - eps) * dy),
                xmin + ((i + eps) * dx),
                ymin + ((j + eps) * dy)
            ),
            nrow = 2,
            dimnames = dimnames (bbox)
            )

            bboxl <- append (bboxl, list (b))
        }
    }
    bboxl
}

final <- list()

for(i in seq_along(place_sf)){

bb_vector <- place_sf[[i]] %>% st_bbox() %>% as.numeric()
bb <- data.frame(min = bb_vector[1:2], max = bb_vector[3:4])
rownames(bb) <- c("x", "y")               
                 
queue <- split_bbox (bb)
result <- list ()

while (length (queue) > 0) {

    print (queue [[1]])

    opres <- NULL
    opres <- try ({
        opq (bbox = queue [[1]], timeout = 25) |>
            add_osm_feature (key = key) |>
            osmdata_sf ()
    })

    if (class (opres) [1] != "try-error") {
        result <- append (result, list (opres))
        queue <- queue [-1]
    } else {
        bboxnew <- split_bbox (queue [[1]])
        queue <- append (bboxnew, queue [-1])
    }
}
final[[i]] <- do.call (c, result)
}

names(final) <- names(place_sf)

return(final)
}


process_osm_list_function <- function(
    list_to_load_and_process, 
    list_to_save_to,
    crs_local_metres){

holding <- list.load(list_to_load_and_process)
holding <- lapply(holding, function(x) 
  bind_rows(x$osm_points, x$osm_lines, x$osm_polygons, x$osm_multilines, x$osm_multipolygons) %>% 
  st_transform(crs = crs_local_metres)) %>% 
  list.save(list_to_save_to)
}
```

```{r display_outputs_figure, out.width = "100%", fig.align = "center", fig.cap = "Software output: Birmingham (left), Bristol (centre) and synthesis (right) display types. Source: authors.", echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, cache=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("graphics/Figure3.png") 

```


During the *Development* phase 
software tools were created
in the R language 
to: download Open Street Maps (OSM) data; 
produce local and regional maps; and
replicate the Bristol and Birmingham styles of 
totems; and 
create a *synthesis* display format, 
which responds to the problem *Definition*. 
OSM and R were chosen to facilitate reuse of the software, 
as these are both open source and freely available. 
Figure \ref{fig:display_outputs_figure} shows 
outputs of the software 
generated for the Gainsborough Square 
case location, 
across the three developed styles: 
replicating the Bristol totem  (left), 
and the Birmingham totem (centre); and 
the developed synthesis display (right).  
These are intended to be printed at A0-scale, 
but the inset in Figure \ref{fig:display_outputs_figure} (bottom left) 
demonstrates how the mapping labels points of interests 
and includes iconographic representation of nearby facilities 
such as bus stops and cafes.  

Higher resolution images of the software outputs are available 
together with the software used to prepare this paper 
on github^[See https://github.com/James-Reynolds/WP5_mobilityHubTools_papers/tree/main/results]. 
Also included in that repository are software outputs for 
the location of the Galway ROBUST e-mobility hub. 
Figure \ref{fig:display_synthesis_details} shows 
selected excerpts from that output^[Full size available at See https://github.com/James-Reynolds/WP5_mobilityHubTools_papers/tree/main/results/galway_synthesis_test.pdf], which are described in the following.  

```{r display_synthesis_details, out.width = "100%", fig.align = "center", fig.cap = "Software output: Birmingham (left), Bristol (centre) and synthesis (right) display types. Source: authors.", echo = FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE, cache=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("graphics/Figure4.png") 

```

The synthesis totem answers 
the five questions developed in the *Definition* phase of this research, 
as indicated in Figure \ref{fig:display_synthesis_details}. 
Question 1 (*What is this?*) is answered by large font 
text ("e-Mobility Hub / Local Travel Point") for viewing from distance, 
and detailed text in the main body of the display.  
Likewise Questions 2 (*Where am I?*) and 3 (*What is here?*) are answered through 
text at various sizes, 
icons and detailed maps.  
Included maps that address Questions 4 (*What is nearby*) 
and 5 (*How can I travel from here?*) 
leverage existing 
map tiles associated with OSM, 
including the the "Transport" 
and "Cycle" tile sets from @Allan:0aa and @Allan:0ab

## Delivery

Software developed in this research 
was assembled into a package of functions, 
as per the guidance provided by @wickham2023r.
This package is available at [https://github.com/James-Reynolds/mobilityHubTools](https://github.com/James-Reynolds/mobilityHubTools). 
It includes functions for 
creating maps (e.g. bristol_local_map.R, synthesis_hub_elements_map.R) 
and totems (e.g. brimingham_totem_pedestal.R, synthesis_totem.R). 
As per the @wickham2023r recommendations 
each function includes a description of variables and other details 
(through a Roxygen Skeleton), 
such that R help files and other package documentation 
are automatically generated.  
Also included in the package are icons (.svg) and 
test data used to generate the Gainsborough Square outputs. 

# Discussion and Conclusions

As briefly noted earlier, 
the research described in this paper is part of the ROBUST project, 
which involves trials of shared electric mobility hubs 
in various locations across Ireland. 
Part of this larger program of research 
will include looking at user behaviour, 
usability 
and related issues 
under real-world conditions. 
Experiments with 
information displays, 
including testing and co-design with users, 
is a direction for future research during ROBUST. 
The research described in this paper, 
however, 
represents an initial 
exploration of this topic 
both through case studies of current practices 
and use of a design-research approach. 

Hub characteristics discovered from the cases studied 
during the first phase of this research 
suggest mobility hubs come in many forms. 
There also appears to be much variability in information displays and user guidance, from comprehensive displays in Bristol and Birmingham 
to linemarking only at some sites in London.
The design problem this study has focused on relates 
specifically to totems and mapping, 
but clearly there are opportunities 
for further research into mobility hub wayfinding 
and information provision. 
As well, 
even those mobility hubs included within the cases 
with more extensive information displays 
do not appear to have fully answered 
the five questions defined here as the 
design problem to be addressed. 

While the synthesis totem display 
output from the *Development* phase 
of the research described here 
does answer all five questions (multiple times), 
further design improvements can clearly be made. 
There may be a need to better understand what facilities and services
might best be included as ‘part’ of a hub, as opposed to those that are mapped as
being ‘nearby’. 
More immediately, 
further development of the
software 
and user testing of the software outputs 
would seem a direction for future research. 

However, the aim of this research 
was to improve understandings 
related to mobility hub informational displays, 
and explore whether it was possible 
to develop software tools 
for implementing mobility hubs at other locations. 
The maps and other details shown in Figure \ref{ref:display_synthesis_details} 
and three different
outputs for the Galway ROBUST hub^[See https://github.com/James-Reynolds/WP5_mobilityHubTools_papers/tree/main/results/galway_synthesis_test.pdf] 
indicate that it is possible to use OSM data 
and mapping tiles 
to produce
mobility hub information displays that might be suitable 
for prototyping, 
public consultation or 
to hand to a graphic designer^[More formally, disproving the (null) hypothesis this paper tests.]. 
The flexibility of R might also 
allow users to adjust layouts, styling and other details as desired.
Likewise, the OSM dataset can be freely accessed and edited by anyone. 
Hence, starting with the developed software 
and a printer tactical urbanists or other grassroots activitist 
might be able define a mobility hub in their own community, 
and keep information displays up to date as circumstances change.
This might raise larger questions, 
such as *who gets to decide what a mobility hub is?*
Perhaps mobility hubs already exist 
wherever there are combinations of: 
railway or electric vehicle charging stations; 
bus or tram stops; 
shared bike docks, 
parking zones or other micro-mobility offerings; 
or other transport-related facilities and services. 
Hopefully the software tools
developed in this study may
help facilitate bottom-up implementation, 
pop-ups or trials, 
or other efforts to 
develop and maintain mobility hubs. 


More generally, 
the research outcomes of 
this study may provide 
insights about current mobility hub information displays developed by practitioners, 
as a step towards identifying 'best practices'.  
Mobility hubs are still a new and evolving approach. 
As per the @Roukouni:2023aa definition, 
a mobility hub needs to provide "integration", 
"seamless, flexible connection" and
"...an enjoyable experience for travelers" 
across multiple modes, 
while also connecting users to 
surrounding services and facilities.  
Overall, it appears that there is 
some way to go in understanding how to deliver upon this, 
even within the narrower confines of information displays 
and other guidance for users at mobility hubs.
